title: What Would Sports Be Like With No Gravity?
summary: Imagine playing basketball where the ball never comes down. Or soccer where a kick sends you flying backward. That is what sports would be like with no gravity. Astronaut Alan Shepard played golf on the Moon. 'First of all, in zero g, Isaac Newton will win every time,' said Les Johnson, a former top scientist at NASA. He means Newton's third law: for every action, there is an equal and opposite reaction. On Earth, gravity and friction hide that rule. In space, it runs the game. With no gravity, up and down stop mattering. The field is no longer flat. Moving is different too. On Earth you can stop and turn fast. In space, once you start moving, you keep going until something stops you. Balls act differently as well. 'There would be no arc, just a straight-line throw,' Johnson said. The best movie example, Johnson says, is Ender's Game from 2013. Its 'Battle Room' is a giant hollow cube where teams play laser-tag games. As NASA's Artemis Program aims to build homes on the Moon, the question is no longer just science fiction.
why_it_matters: If you ever play sports on the Moon, you will need a whole new way to play.

background_read: Gravity pulls everything on Earth downward, and it shapes every sport: it decides how balls arc through the air and which way is up.
In zero gravity, there is almost no gravity, so objects float and keep moving until something stops them.
NASA's Artemis Program aims to build homes on the Moon, where people would live and work for long periods.

WHAT: Sports in zero gravity would break every rule we know.
WHERE: On the Moon and in space.
WHY: Without gravity, balls do not arc and players keep drifting until something stops them.
